So, two people have different genes. But what is it in the subsequent processes that results in different colors? Is the hair physically different? How can a person's hair color change as they get older?
What exactly (beyond differing genes) causes different people to have different hair color?

The two pigments eumelanin and pheomelanin give hair color, different variances in these pigments cause different colors. Pheomelanin colors hair orange-yellow, while eumelanin colors them black and brown and generally governs the brightness of the hair. White/gray hair by aging is a result of gradual loss of these pigments. This Wikipedia page covers everything you should want to know well.

Because I like to specialize in evolution, I would be remiss not to include a short diatribe on the evolution of hair color. (You don't have to read this but I got curious so I decided to share it with anyone who bothers to read it). The cradle of civilization is in Africa, so likewise hair/skin color would have to be dark in order to block out ultraviolet light. We see this complexion in our ape ancestors and in modern people of African descent. As humans migrated north, the selective pressure for dark complexions waned, and was even selected against as lighter skin/hair allowed for more efficient absorption of Vitamin D. This was problematic for humans, especially those in northern climates where the sun isn't out very much throughout the year, because we derive our Vitamin D almost exclusively from the sun, because we didn't have the ever-important nectar of the gods that the modern world is blessed with today. This page goes into more detail.

We see the vast majority of hair colors today because the genes controlling hair color (as little as we know about them) are generally accepted to be multiple, allowing for more mutations and more variance.
